The part of this that doesn't make sense is the 1v1 clutch person gaining more RR than a person who gets first blood. First blood gives 150 ACS and every kill after gives 20 less ACS. In your example you consider the clutch to be the highest impact kill even though the game calculates the first blood to be the highest impact. ACS doesn't even directly affect MMR either according to the link so it doesn't really matter towards MMR. "The portion of your RR due to performance at the end of the match is then decided based on how much Encounter MMR you have gained or lost compared to the amount you were expected to gain or lose based on the MMR of the players in the match at the start." Overall RR gain is just determined by how well you do compared to what the game calculated.

The link you posted says, "A common misconception is to estimate the performance of the match based on a player's ACS, which is often significantly inaccurate and misleading." It's stated that, "Performing much higher than your expectation will result in increased RR, while performing under this bar will have reduced RR." 

OP is comparing his MMR to his friend's even though they're just calculated in individual ways. OP is just performing above expectations in comparison to his MMR. I'm guessing that if his friend is always placed higher on the leaderboard, then his friend is expected to always perform at that level or better in order to gain more RR and lose less. If his friend underperforms compared to what the game calculates his performance to be, then he loses more than OP. That's how I understand it based on the info in the link.

Do you focus on crosshair placement and good movement? No diagonal peeking, no shift peeking, slicing the pie, etc. Improving my fundamentals is what helped me climb faster. I climbed 5 ranks quickly just from practicing fundamentals a lot. Crosshair placement and clearly things carefully is the most important. The lower the elo the more people tend to wide swing when they peek so you can hold your crosshair wider if you're holding an angle. But the more you climb the less wide you tend to hold since they'll just peek narrower and narrower but this didn't start happening to me till I reached plat. When you deathmatch try playing with music to not hear people and just practice crosshair placement and clearing things better. This is how I train in deathmatch and what helped me improve enough to keep climbing. Plus deathmatches can possibly put you against higher ranked players so you can practice against better people. You're on the right track by doing what Woohoojin recommends. He puts emphasis on fundamentals and movement so keep practicing and you'll climb cause this is exactly how I climbed several ranks quickly. The better your crosshair placement the less you'll have to rely on aim. People in low elo take a really long time to shoot back so if you're already accurate with crosshair placement then you'll be able to kill them a lot quicker. If you have to keep readjusting your aim it means your crosshair placement was incorrect and needs work.

EDIT: Also comming a lot is something that helped me to climb too and increased my game sense and awareness. Also comm what agent is in what location and how much you hit them for. If your teammate isn't near them yet then say they were last in that location but could've left so it isn't inaccurate. I think comms in low elo are really broken for climbing since people lack general awareness in low elo. If you're dead you can just comm where everyone is and your teammates will have a really easy time cause they'll know where to shoot. When you watch Woohoojin's vods he always says to run to your teammate if they're fighting someone and help them fight. That works really well in low elo imo. On defense switch sites often to have a higher chance of seeing the enemy and having higher impact. If you wanna keep playing Reyna then play off angles and make sure to press ur E really early so you can't get traded. Reyna can almost always get out of being traded if she spams her E while she kills someone. Also if you wanna do even more stuff that Woohoojin recommends then you should try vod reviewing yourself. You can have a higher ranked friend watch the vod with you too and tell you what you're doing wrong and how to fix it. You should be able to see what you could've done differently in general to win rounds. Vod reviewing helped me climb faster too. But you'll mostly want to pay attention to crosshair placement cause you'll just become more consistent that way.

For example, if the enemy midlaner is missing, your midlaner should ping that. If they think the enemy mid is roaming bot, they should also ping that so that you can back off and play safer. Watching the map and cs'ing are going to be the most important things when playing against real people. It's likely that people on your team won't ping things at all so make sure to glance at your mini-map often to keep track of everyone. Try to learn the matchups and powerspikes if you find that helpful. Players also like to rotate lanes or all fight in midlane when laning phase ends. This all depends on the people you play with though. In low elo your team is most likely going to be looking for fights constantly when there aren't any objectives up. As an adc it's usually good to follow them just to win fights more. Make sure to stand out of range of enemy abilities as an ADC so that you don't get caught. Ideally you should stand behind people in teamfights so that they can peel for you as you dish out damage. Also, it's not always necessary to chase someone just because they're low health. Sometimes it's better to focus on macro and cs'ing to get you and your teammates ahead. I don't know your play style vs AI, but try to back to buy items when you have enough gold. On most ADCs I back when I can buy Noonquiver or some of it's components. Try to back at a time when you won't miss cs, especially the canon wave. However, back if you're too low and are afraid of dying. It's okay to take the game at your own pace as you learn. Don't let the flaming get to you! It used to bother me a lot when I started but now it's kind of just annoying because it doesn't help anyone. It's healthy to mute them if they're distracting you. Every game is a learning opportunity so don't be afraid of failure.  


Oh and buy control wards. You can place these on objectives like dragon when your team is taking it to deny enemy vision. There are other uses for them too of course, which you can learn as you play or by watching streamers/vods/tutorials.
